Notes

General Approach to Any Adrenal Lesion

FIXED FORMAT
History → Examination → Blood tests → Imaging → Management
Notes

★ Core Exam Framework for an Adrenal Mass

StepContent
1. HistoryHypertension? Headache? Palpitations? Sweating? Muscle cramps/weakness? Polyuria/polydipsia? Weight gain/Cushing features? Steroid use? Previous cancer? Family history?
2. ExaminationBP, HR, sweating, cushingoid features/central obesity, abdominal mass only if very large
3. LabsCBC, renal/liver function, Na⁺/K⁺, metanephrines, aldosterone + renin/ARR, cortisol ± further endocrine tests
4. ImagingCT adrenal protocol = key standard imaging; MRI for selected large/complex lesions; PET-CT when malignancy/metastasis remains uncertain
5. MANAGEMENT DEPENDS ON THE SCENARIO
Small nonfunctional benign incidentaloma → observe
>4 cm / significant growth → adrenalectomy
Pheochromocytoma → α-blockade → β-blockade if needed → adrenalectomy
Conn syndrome → correct electrolytes/BP ± spironolactone → adrenalectomy when unilateral surgical disease
Cushing/adrenal cortisol lesion → endocrine optimization ± surgery per cause
ACC → en bloc oncologic resection
Possible adrenal metastasis → stage + PET/selective biopsy only if it will change management

Conn Syndrome — Primary Hyperaldosteronism

Clinical Picture

Typical scenario: hypertension, hypokalemia, ± hypernatremia, muscle cramps/weakness, polyuria/polydipsia.

LABORATORY PATTERN
↑ Aldosterone, ↓ Renin, ↑ ARR (>30), ↓ K⁺. Metanephrines/cortisol may be normal when this is an isolated aldosterone-producing lesion.

Notes

2. Primary Hyperaldosteronism — Conn Syndrome

Tests: aldosterone, renin, aldosterone:renin ratio (ARR).

TYPICAL PATTERN
↑ Aldosterone, ↓ Renin, ARR >30 → suggestive of Conn syndrome, hypokalemia, may have hypernatremia. Endocrinology may perform aldosterone suppression testing for confirmation.
Diagnosis is primarily biochemical; CT localizes the lesion rather than making the hormonal diagnosis.

Notes

Management

Before definitive treatment: correct hypokalemia, correct significant electrolyte abnormalities, control hypertension.

MEDICAL THERAPY
Spironolactone (aldosterone antagonist) — helps preserve/increase potassium and control BP; may be used medically/preoperatively.

Definitive treatment: for an appropriate unilateral adrenal aldosterone-producing lesion → adrenalectomy.

YOUNGER PATIENTS — CAUTION
In approximately 35–40-year-old patients, remember hyperaldosteronism may result from bilateral adrenal hyperplasia rather than a single unilateral adenoma. Before removing one adrenal, ensure the unilateral lesion is truly responsible rather than assuming every visible nodule is the cause.
Notes

Management

Initial management depends on the cause and endocrine assessment. Surgical treatment is considered when there is an appropriate surgically correctable adrenal source or failure/unsuitability of medical treatment.

If adrenal tissue is completely removed bilaterally → the patient requires long-term/lifelong steroid replacement.

3. Cushing Syndrome

Screening: 24-hour cortisol assessment, cortisol testing ± dexamethasone suppression test.

ACTH HELPS LOCALIZE THE SOURCE
Adrenal cortisol-producing lesion → low ACTH (negative feedback). ACTH-dependent causes → ACTH not suppressed. Detailed endocrine localization is not the main surgical focus.

Notes

Pheochromocytoma Management

DEFINITIVE TREATMENT
Adrenalectomy, usually laparoscopic when appropriate. However, never proceed directly to surgery without controlling the catecholamine effects.
Notes

Preoperative Preparation

★ HIGH-YIELD: Α BEFORE Β
1. α-blockade FIRST — vasodilation, control hypertension, prepare for surgery. Several weeks of BP optimization before surgery.
2. β-blocker only AFTER adequate α-blockade — used mainly for tachycardia/palpitations/symptom control.
Giving β-blockade first risks leaving unopposed α-adrenergic vasoconstriction, worsening hypertension.
α BEFORE β. β-blockade first leaves α-vasoconstriction unopposed → worse hypertension.
Notes

Intraoperative Principles

Tumor manipulation can release large amounts of catecholamines.

PhaseExpected Change
During adrenal dissectionManipulation → marked hypertension; surgeon + anesthetist must actively anticipate/manage BP changes, possibly with intraoperative antihypertensive/vasodilator therapy
Adrenal vein controlEarly control/ligation limits further catecholamine release
After venous ligation/tumor removalCatecholamine level suddenly falls → patient may develop significant hypotension → treat with fluid resuscitation ± hemodynamic support
★ SURGICAL PRINCIPLE
Expect hypertension during manipulation → hypotension after adrenal vein ligation/tumor removal.

Notes

Functional Assessment in Suspected ACC

Assess cortical hormone production: cortisol, aldosterone, androgens, estrogens. Also ensure a catecholamine-secreting lesion such as pheochromocytoma has been excluded before intervention — ACC may be functional, so hormonal assessment remains necessary even when the main concern is malignancy.

Slide 23

Notes

Adrenal Biopsy — Very Important

★ DO NOT ROUTINELY BIOPSY
Biopsy is considered only in selected situations: (1) lesion is nonfunctional — especially pheochromocytoma must first be excluded; (2) imaging/PET suggests possible metastasis or another diagnosis; (3) the biopsy result will actually change management.

Do NOT biopsy simply because: the mass is large; it is already clearly resectable and surgery is indicated; suspected adrenocortical carcinoma will be managed surgically regardless.

EXAM PRINCIPLE
Ask: "Will the biopsy result change management?" If not → biopsy is unnecessary.
Don't routinely biopsy an adrenal mass. Only if non-functional (phaeo excluded first), imaging suggests metastasis/another diagnosis, AND the result will change management. Never because it is large.

Notes

Adrenocortical Carcinoma (ACC)

RARE, AGGRESSIVE
Approximately 1–2% of adrenal lesions. Often diagnosed late; more common in older patients; poor prognosis when advanced. Usually a large adrenal mass, often >6 cm at diagnosis. May invade kidney, retroperitoneal structures, lymph nodes, other adjacent organs. A very large tumor may be palpable.
Notes

Management

DEFINITIVE TREATMENT
Surgical resection when resectable, aiming for en bloc resection — tumor removed together with any directly involved surrounding structures/organs as one oncologic specimen, rather than shelling the mass out.
★ HIGH-YIELD
Suspected resectable ACC → do NOT routinely biopsy; proceed toward oncologic resection if appropriate. Biopsy usually does not change management when a large resectable adrenal malignancy is already suspected.
Notes

Adrenal Metastasis

Always consider metastasis when an adrenal lesion occurs in a patient with a previous malignancy — e.g. a patient with breast cancer years earlier + new adrenal lesion.
Notes

Assessment

Restage/search for metastatic disease (e.g. chest/abdomen and other appropriate sites) Reassess the original primary when clinically appropriate

1 2 3 4

Perform the usual functional adrenal work-up

Characterize the adrenal lesion with CT adrenal protocol

Notes

PET-CT in an Indeterminate Adrenal Lesion

Especially useful when the patient has a previous cancer and CT does not clearly distinguish benign lesion from metastasis.

PET ResultInterpretation
No significant uptakeSupports a benign/non-active lesion — manage per incidentaloma principles if otherwise appropriate
Increased uptakeMay represent malignancy or inflammation/infection — uptake alone is not completely specific
Isolated Adrenal Metastasis
If metastatic disease is isolated to the adrenal and the patient is otherwise suitable, adrenal metastasectomy/resection may offer prognostic benefit in selected patients. Widespread disease involving multiple organs represents advanced/stage IV disease and is managed differently.

Notes

Focused History

Assess symptoms suggesting a functional adrenal lesion:

SyndromeKey Symptoms
HypertensionNewly diagnosed? Controlled/uncontrolled? Resistant? Number of antihypertensive medications?
PheochromocytomaHeadache, palpitations, sweating ± hypertensive attacks/crises
Conn/hyperaldosteronismHypertension, muscle cramps/weakness, polyuria/polydipsia → suggest hypokalemia
Cushing syndromeWeight gain, easy bruising, mood changes, central obesity/cushingoid features
Ask about exogenous steroid use when Cushing features are present. If any symptom is positive → explore it further rather than only documenting yes/no.
Notes

Family / Cancer History

Ask about family history of endocrine/adrenal tumors or cancer, and previous personal malignancy, since adrenal lesions may represent metastases.

PRIMARIES THAT MAY METASTASIZE TO ADRENAL
Lung cancer, breast cancer, renal cell carcinoma, thyroid cancer, melanoma/skin malignancy.

Pheochromocytoma may be part of MEN2: medullary thyroid carcinoma → ↑ calcitonin, may cause chronic diarrhea; hyperparathyroidism → hypercalcemia.

Notes

Adrenal Incidentaloma

DEFINITION
A lesion discovered by chance in a patient without symptoms suggesting a functional adrenal tumor. Before calling it a simple incidentaloma: (1) assess for hormonal function, (2) assess malignancy risk/history, (3) characterize it radiologically.
ScenarioManagement
>4 cmAdrenalectomy — malignancy risk approximately 5–7%
<4 cm + nonfunctional + benign appearingObservation/follow-up — repeat CT at ~6 months, then interval/annual follow-up if stable
Growth >1 cm/year during follow-upConcerning for malignancy → surgical removal
EXAM POINT
An adrenal lesion >4 cm → do not biopsy simply because it is large; management is adrenalectomy if surgical criteria are met.

Notes

Mastery Checklist

1 ↓K⁺ + hypertension ± ↑Na⁺ should immediately trigger consideration of Conn syndrome
2 Adrenal hormonal diagnosis is biochemical (metanephrines, ARR, cortisol) — CT localizes the lesion, it doesn't make the diagnosis
3 Incidentaloma >4cm goes to adrenalectomy (~5–7% malignancy risk); <4cm nonfunctional/benign-appearing is observed with repeat CT at ~6 months; growth >1cm/year is concerning
4 A large adrenal mass is never a reason by itself to biopsy — size doesn't change the biopsy decision
5 ★ Pheochromocytoma prep is always α-blockade first, then β-blockade if needed — never β first (risks unopposed α vasoconstriction)
6 ★ Expect hypertension during pheochromocytoma tumor manipulation, then hypotension after adrenal vein ligation/tumor removal — plan fluids/support accordingly
7 In a 35–40 year old with hyperaldosteronism, consider bilateral adrenal hyperplasia before assuming a visible nodule is a unilateral Conn adenoma
8 Bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing's requires lifelong steroid replacement
9 ACC is typically large (>6cm) at diagnosis and still needs functional hormone workup (cortisol/aldosterone/androgens/estrogens) plus pheo exclusion before intervention
10 ★ Suspected resectable ACC should go straight to en bloc oncologic resection — do not biopsy first, since it won't change management
11 Any adrenal lesion in a patient with prior malignancy should trigger restaging and consideration of metastasis, not just incidentaloma workup
12 PET uptake is not fully specific — it can reflect malignancy OR inflammation/infection, not just cancer
13 The universal biopsy question: "will this result change management?" — if not, don't biopsy

Adrenals

Adrenal Anatomy and Surgical Considerations
  • Weight and Position:
  • Combined adrenal weight: 7–12 grams.
  • Right adrenal gland: Posterior and lateral to the vena cava, superior to the kidney.
  • Left adrenal gland: Medial to the superior pole of the kidney, lateral to the aorta, and posterior to the pancreas.
  • Vascular Anatomy:
  • Adrenal veins:
    • Right adrenal vein: Short (2–5 mm), drains into the vena cava.
    • Left adrenal vein: Longer, drains into the left renal vein after receiving the inferior phrenic vein.
    • Variants: Multiple or anomalous veins occur in 9%–17% of cases, especially with pheochromocytomas and larger tumors.
  • Adrenal arteries: Small, multiple, and variable, typically arising from the inferior phrenic artery, the aorta, and the renal artery.
Indications for Adrenal Surgery
  • Main Cause: Hypersecretory states (excessive hormone secretion).
  • Diagnosis: 1. Confirm hormone excess (cortisol, aldosterone, or catecholamines) via blood or urine tests. 2. Measure levels of trophic hormones (e.g., ACTH or renin).
    • Suppressed trophic hormone + high adrenal hormone → autonomous adrenal secretion confirmed.
  • 3. Assess autonomy to differentiate:
    • Hyperplasia: Partial control by feedback mechanisms.
    • Adenomas: Greater independence.
    • Cancers: Minimal or no feedback control.
  • Note: If the primary problem is elsewhere (e.g., pituitary in Cushing disease), adrenal surgery is not indicated.
Principles of Adrenal Surgery

1. Confirm Diagnosis and Localization before surgery.

2. Prepare the Patient to handle metabolic challenges.

3. Monitor and manage potential metabolic crises during and after surgery.

Surgical Approaches to Adrenal Tumors
  • Preoperative Imaging: CT and MRI allow precise tumor localization, minimizing the need for general exploration.
  • Laparoscopic Adrenalectomy (Preferred):
  • Transabdominal approach:
    • Medial rotation of organs (spleen/pancreas on left; liver on right).
    • Better for larger tumors.
  • Retroperitoneal approach:
    • High insufflation pressure creates space and reduces bleeding.
    • Better for bilateral tumors or patients with abdominal adhesions.
  • Choice of approach often depends on surgeon preference.
  • Open Adrenalectomy (Traditional):
  • Indicated for:
    • Very large tumors (>8–10 cm).
    • Locally invasive cancers needing lymph node or adjacent organ resection.
  • Techniques:
    • Anterior approach (midline, subcostal, or "L" incision): Allows wide exposure but causes more pain and complications.
    • Posterior approach (through 11th or 12th rib bed): Largely replaced by laparoscopic surgery.
    • Thoracoabdominal incision: Reserved for very large tumors needing access above the diaphragm.
  • Preference: Laparoscopic surgery is strongly preferred due to faster recovery, less pain, and fewer complications.
Primary Aldosteronism
Overview
  • Characterized by hypertension (with or without hypokalemia), elevated aldosterone secretion, and suppressed plasma renin activity.
  • Leads to metabolic alkalosis, mild hypernatremia, and symptoms related to hypokalemia (e.g., weakness, polyuria, paresthesia, cramps).
Pathophysiology
  • Aldosterone increases sodium retention, decreases potassium, expands extracellular fluid, and raises blood pressure.
  • Normally regulated by the renin-angiotensin system and transiently by ACTH.
  • Primary aldosteronism: autonomous aldosterone secretion (high aldosterone, low renin).
  • Secondary hyperaldosteronism: elevated aldosterone due to increased renin (e.g., renovascular disease, cirrhosis).
Subtypes
  • Common:
  • Aldosterone-producing adenomas (aldosteronomas).
  • Idiopathic hyperaldosteronism (bilateral adrenal hyperplasia).
  • Rare:
  • Unilateral adrenal hyperplasia.
  • Familial hyperaldosteronism (FH) types I, II, and III.
  • Aldosterone-secreting adrenal carcinoma.
Clinical Features
Symptoms
  • Often due to hypokalemia: malaise, muscle weakness, polyuria, polydipsia, cramps, paresthesia.
  • Severe cases: tetany, hypokalemic paralysis.
  • Hypertension: typically moderate to severe, often resistant to treatment. Edema is uncommon unless renal failure develops.
Laboratory Findings
1. Screening
  • Indications: hypertension with hypokalemia, resistant hypertension, adrenal incidentalomas.
  • Test: Plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC)/Plasma renin activity (PRA) ratio.
  • PAC/PRA > 20, elevated PAC (>15 ng/dL typically), suppressed PRA (<1 ng/mL/hr) suggests primary aldosteronism.
  • Medications (e.g., ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone) must be discontinued before testing if possible.
2. Confirmatory Testing
  • Sodium loading tests:
  • Oral high-sodium diet or intravenous saline infusion.
  • Failure to suppress aldosterone (>12–14 µg/24h in urine, or PAC >10 ng/mL after saline infusion) confirms diagnosis.
Differential Diagnosis
  • Differentiate aldosteronoma (surgically treatable) from idiopathic hyperaldosteronism (treated medically).
  • Aldosteronoma: younger patients, more severe hypertension/hypokalemia, higher aldosterone secretion.
  • Familial Hyperaldosteronism (FH):
  • Type I (glucocorticoid-remediable): treated with steroids.
  • Types II and III: genetics less clear; FH-III due to KCNJ5 mutations.
Tumor Localization
  • CT or MRI imaging identifies tumors but can miss small lesions.
  • Adrenal vein sampling:
  • Gold standard if imaging is unclear (e.g., bilateral masses, small tumors).
  • Measures aldosterone-to-cortisol ratio from each adrenal vein to determine laterality.
  • High technical skill required; about 90% success rate.
Complications
  • Uncontrolled hypertension: renal failure, stroke, myocardial infarction.
  • Severe hypokalemia: weakness, paralysis, arrhythmias (especially with digitalis use).
Treatment
A. Surgical Treatment
  • Unilateral adrenalectomy for aldosteronomas:
  • Preoperative control with spironolactone (aldosterone antagonist).
  • Preferred surgical method: laparoscopic adrenalectomy (transabdominal or retroperitoneal).
  • Total adrenalectomy is preferred over partial resection.
  • Rarely, short-term fludrocortisone may be needed postoperatively for transient aldosterone deficiency.
B. Medical Treatment
  • For idiopathic hyperaldosteronism or non-surgical candidates:
  • Spironolactone (initially 200–400 mg/day, then maintenance 100– 150 mg/day).
  • Eplerenone: selective mineralocorticoid receptor blocker with fewer side effects.
  • Amiloride: potassium-sparing diuretic as alternative or adjunct.
  • Other antihypertensives as needed (ACE inhibitors, calcium channel blockers).
Prognosis
  • Without treatment: risk of stroke, myocardial infarction, renal failure.
  • After adrenalectomy:
  • Potassium normalization in almost all patients.
  • Cure of hypertension in about 50%; residual hypertension is easier to control.
  • Surgery is preferred over lifelong medical treatment, when possible, especially due to the side effects and compliance issues with long-term medications.
Pheochromocytoma
Overview
  • Tumors of the adrenal medulla (or related extra-adrenal chromaffin tissue — paragangliomas).
  • Secrete epinephrine or norepinephrine, causing sustained or episodic hypertension and catecholamine excess symptoms.
  • Accounts for:
  • <0.1% of all hypertension cases.
  • ~5% of adrenal incidentalomas.
  • About 10% of pheochromocytomas and 40% of paragangliomas are malignant.
  • One-third are associated with hereditary syndromes (MEN2, NF1, VHL, hereditary PPGL).
Clinical Features
Symptoms and Signs
  • Classic triad: Episodic headache, sweating, and palpitations.
  • Other symptoms: Anxiety, tremor, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, constipation, visual blurring.
  • Signs: Tachycardia, pallor, excessive sweating, postural hypotension.
  • Hypertension:
  • 90% of patients.
  • May be sustained or episodic.
  • Metabolic effects: Hypermetabolism, hyperglycemia due to catecholamine effects.
Special Considerations
  • Children: Higher rates of multiple or extra-adrenal tumors.
  • Pregnancy: Extremely dangerous if undiagnosed, requiring MRI (not CT) and careful management.
Diagnosis
Biochemical Testing
  • Plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines (high sensitivity and specificity).
  • Preparation:
  • Discontinue interfering drugs (e.g., tricyclics, labetalol, MAOIs).
  • Perform tests ideally in a supine fasting state.
Imaging
  • After biochemical confirmation:
  • CT or MRI: Main modalities (MRI better for avoiding radiation).
  • MIBG scan: Useful for detecting multiple, metastatic, or extra- adrenal tumors.
  • PET-CT (e.g., 68Ga-DOTATATE): Most sensitive for SDHB-related metastatic disease.
  • Biopsy and venous sampling: Contraindicated due to risk of hypertensive crisis.
Differential Diagnosis
  • Hyperthyroidism.
  • Acute anxiety/panic attacks.
  • Carcinoid syndrome (elevated 5-HIAA levels).
  • Labile essential hypertension.
  • Pheochromocytoma must be considered carefully in pregnancy and in cases of unexplained severe hypertension.
Treatment
Medical Management (Preoperative)
  • α-adrenergic blockade:
  • Start as soon as diagnosis is made.
  • Preferred agent: Phenoxybenzamine (non-selective, long-acting α- blocker).
  • Alternatives: Doxazosin (selective α1️-blocker).
  • β-blockers:
  • Only after α-blockade is established to prevent unopposed α- adrenergic stimulation.
  • Metyrosine: Inhibits catecholamine synthesis, used in some severe cases.
Surgical Management
  • Definitive treatment: Surgical removal.
  • Laparoscopic adrenalectomy: Preferred for small (<5–6 cm) adrenal tumors.
  • Open surgery: Needed for larger (>8–10 cm), invasive, or extra- adrenal tumors.
  • Intraoperative considerations:
  • Continuous arterial pressure monitoring.
  • Ready availability of nitroprusside (for hypertension) and β-blockers (for arrhythmias).
Complications
  • Before surgery: Hypertensive crisis, arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, stroke, renal failure.
  • During/after surgery:
  • Hypertensive crisis during tumor manipulation.
  • Severe hypotension after tumor removal (due to sudden catecholamine withdrawal).
  • Hypoglycemia after tumor resection.
  • Proper preoperative preparation with α-blockade minimizes risks.
Prognosis
  • Untreated pheochromocytoma: High mortality from hypertensive crises and cardiovascular disease.
  • Surgical treatment:
  • Operative mortality: 0–3%.
  • Long-term cure rate is high with adequate preoperative preparation.
  • Recurrence/metastasis:
  • Possible even years later, especially in hereditary cases.
  • Lifelong follow-up required.
  • Genetic counseling:
  • Recommended for all patients due to high hereditary component (mutations: RET, VHL, SDHB, SDHD, others).
Hypercortisolism (Cushing Disease & Cushing Syndrome)
Overview
  • Cushing syndrome: Chronic glucocorticoid excess from various causes.
  • Cushing disease: A subtype caused by ACTH-secreting pituitary adenomas.
  • Other causes:
  • ACTH-independent: Adrenocortical adenomas, carcinomas, or hyperplasia.
  • Ectopic ACTH syndrome: From tumors (e.g., small-cell lung cancer, carcinoid tumors).
Clinical Features
Symptoms and Signs
  • Typical features:
  • Facial plethora, moon face, dorsocervical (buffalo hump) and supraclavicular fat pads.
  • Truncal obesity, purple striae, easy bruising, hirsutism, acne, impotence/amenorrhea.
  • Muscle weakness, depression/psychosis, osteopenia/osteoporosis.
  • Hypertension, hyperglycemia.
  • In children: Growth retardation is common.
Pathologic Findings
  • Cushing disease: Adrenal glands mildly enlarged (~25 g).
  • Ectopic ACTH: Marked adrenal hyperplasia (up to 100 g).
  • Adrenal adenomas: Usually >3 cm, golden-yellow, sometimes difficult to distinguish from carcinomas.
  • Adrenocortical carcinomas: Very large (>5 cm), invasive, and often metastatic.
  • Rare forms: Macronodular hyperplasia, pigmented nodular disease (linked to Carney complex).
Diagnosis
Step 1: Confirm Hypercortisolism
  • Initial Screening Tests: 1. Overnight dexamethasone suppression test:
    • 1 mg dexamethasone at 11 PM; cortisol measured at 8 AM.
    • Cortisol ≤ 1️.8 µg/dL usually rules out Cushing syndrome.
  • 2. 24-hour urinary free cortisol: Measures free cortisol secretion.
  • 3. Late-night salivary cortisol: Detects loss of cortisol diurnal rhythm.
  • False positives: Depression, alcoholism, obesity, sleep apnea, estrogen use.
Step 2: Determine the Cause
  • Plasma ACTH measurement:
  • Suppressed ACTH → Adrenal tumor (ACTH-independent).
  • Normal/Elevated ACTH → ACTH-dependent (pituitary or ectopic).
  • Distinguishing Pituitary from Ectopic ACTH:
  • Pituitary MRI: Identify pituitary adenomas.
  • Inferior Petrosal Sinus Sampling (IPSS):
    • Gold standard if MRI is inconclusive.
    • Central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient >2 at baseline (or >3 after CRH) confirms pituitary source.
Imaging Studies
  • Thin-section CT or MRI:
  • Adrenal tumors/hyperplasia: CT/MRI.
  • Pituitary tumors: MRI of the sella.
  • Occult ectopic tumors: Chest/abdomen CT or PET-CT.
Complications
  • From hypercortisolism:
  • Cardiovascular disease, stroke, infections, severe muscle wasting, psychosis, thromboembolism.
  • Postoperative risks:
  • Pulmonary complications, poor wound healing.
  • Nelson syndrome:
  • Aggressive ACTH-secreting pituitary tumor after bilateral adrenalectomy.
Treatment
A. Surgical Treatment
  • Pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease):
  • Transsphenoidal microsurgery is first-line.
  • If unsuccessful: pituitary irradiation, medical therapy, or bilateral adrenalectomy.
  • Adrenal adenomas/carcinomas:
  • Unilateral adrenalectomy (laparoscopic preferred for benign tumors).
  • Open surgery if carcinoma is suspected (to avoid capsule rupture).
  • Bilateral adrenalectomy:
  • Reserved for occult ectopic ACTH or bilateral adrenal disease.
B. Medical Therapy
  • Used when surgery is not feasible or as a bridge:
  • Steroidogenesis inhibitors: Ketoconazole (first-line), metyrapone, aminoglutethimide.
  • Glucocorticoid receptor blocker: Mifepristone (RU-486).
  • Adrenolytic agent: Mitotane (for adrenocortical carcinoma).
  • Others: Pasireotide (somatostatin analog), cabergoline (dopamine agonist).
C. Postoperative Management
  • Hydrocortisone replacement:
  • High doses initially; taper gradually to maintenance (~15–20 mg/day).
  • Fludrocortisone:
  • Added if bilateral adrenalectomy is performed.
  • Stress-dose steroids:
  • Needed during stress (infection, surgery) to prevent adrenal crisis.
Prognosis
  • Benign tumors: Excellent with proper surgery.
  • Cushing disease: Good if pituitary tumor is completely resected; recurrence possible.
  • Adrenocortical carcinoma and ectopic ACTH tumors: Poor prognosis.
  • Long-term follow-up: Necessary for all patients due to recurrence risk.
Virilizing Adrenal Tumors
Overview
  • Rare in adults; more common adrenal tumors secrete aldosterone or cortisol.
  • In women, virilization is more often due to ovarian tumors than adrenal tumors.
  • Virilization results from adrenal hypersecretion of:
  • Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), DHEA sulfate (DHEAS), and androstenedione.
  • These are converted peripherally to testosterone and dihydrotestosterone.
  • Rarely, tumors secrete testosterone only.
Malignancy
  • Differentiating benign from malignant tumors histologically is difficult.
  • 70% of virilizing adrenal tumors exhibit malignant behavior.
  • Adrenocortical carcinomas:
  • Usually large, invasive, and secrete multiple steroids (often cortisol + androgens → Cushing syndrome + virilization).
  • Prognosis worsens with tumors >100 g.
Clinical Features
  • Signs of Virilization:
  • Hirsutism, male-pattern baldness, acne, deepened voice, male musculature, clitoromegaly, amenorrhea/irregular menses, increased libido.
  • In children:
  • Rapid linear growth, advanced bone age.
  • Tumors are less likely to be malignant compared to adults.
Diagnosis and Treatment
  • Imaging: CT and MRI.
  • Definitive treatment: Surgical resection.
Related Condition
  • Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH):
  • Autosomal recessive disorder.
  • 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for 90% of cases.
  • Results in cortisol deficiency → ACTH overproduction → androgen excess.
  • Treatment: Glucocorticoid ± mineralocorticoid replacement.
Feminizing Adrenal Tumors
Overview
  • Extremely rare and almost always carcinomas.
  • Occur mainly in men (causing feminization) or girls (causing precocious puberty).
  • Women may present with vaginal bleeding.
Hormone Secretion
  • Normally, the adrenal cortex does not synthesize estrogens.
  • Feminizing adrenal tumors hypersecrete estrogens and often other hormones.
Diagnosis
  • Elevated plasma estrogens.
  • Must rule out ovarian tumors and exogenous estrogen use.
Treatment
  • Definitive treatment: Surgical excision.
  • Prognosis: Generally poor.
Adrenocortical Carcinoma
Overview
  • Rare malignancy of the adrenal cortex.
  • >50% of patients present with symptoms of hormone hypersecretion:
  • Most commonly Cushing syndrome and/or virilization.
  • Feminizing or aldosterone-secreting carcinomas are rare.
  • Hormone excess may sometimes be subclinical and detected only through biochemical studies.
  • Tumor may be palpable at presentation.
Tumor Characteristics
  • Mean tumor diameter: 12 cm (range: 3–30 cm).
  • Highly aggressive:
  • Invades surrounding tissues.
  • About 50% have metastases (to lung, liver, etc.) at diagnosis.
Prognosis
  • Depends heavily on tumor stage at diagnosis:
  • Stage I: 66% 5-year survival
  • Stage II: 58%
  • Stage III: 24%
  • Stage IV: 0%
  • Complete surgical resection (R0) offers the only chance for cure.
  • Even after complete resection, recurrence is common due to micrometastases.
Treatment
Surgery
  • Primary and most important treatment.
  • Open surgery preferred for large tumors or suspected malignancy.
  • Laparoscopic approach acceptable initially for small tumors if surgeon is highly experienced, but low threshold for conversion to open surgery.
  • Resection of adjacent involved organs and suspicious lymph nodes should be done if cancer is suspected.
  • Reoperation for local recurrence may prolong survival.
  • Patients with distant metastases at diagnosis usually die within a year; adrenalectomy does not improve survival in such cases.
Medical Therapy
  • Mitotane (adrenolytic agent):
  • Controls endocrine symptoms in ~50% of patients.
  • Can induce tumor regression in unresectable cases.
  • Adjuvant mitotane after complete resection improves recurrence- free survival.
  • Side effects: Gastrointestinal symptoms, dizziness, weakness, somnolence.
  • Chemotherapy:
  • FIRM-ACT trial: Combination of etoposide, doxorubicin, and cisplatin plus mitotane improved response and progression-free survival compared to mitotane + streptozocin.
  • No significant difference in overall survival between regimens.
Radiation Therapy
  • Limited role:
  • Mainly used for palliation, especially for bone metastases.
  • Adjuvant radiation may improve local control but does not improve overall survival.
Adrenal Incidentalomas
Overview
  • Incidentalomas are adrenal tumors found incidentally during imaging (CT, MRI, ultrasound) done for unrelated reasons.
  • Incidence:
  • Found in 4% of CT scans and 6% of random autopsies.
  • Risk increases with age.
Types of Lesions Found
  • 90% are presumed nonfunctioning cortical adenomas.
  • Others include:
  • Subclinical Cushing syndrome: 6.4%
  • Pheochromocytoma: 3.1%
  • Adrenocortical carcinoma: 1.8%
  • Metastatic carcinoma: 0.7%
  • Aldosteronoma: 0.6%
  • Other benign lesions: Simple adrenal cysts, myelolipomas, adrenal hemorrhage.
Clinical Evaluation
Goals
  • Determine if the tumor is: 1. Functioning (hormone-secreting). 2. Malignant.
Workup
1. History and Physical Examination:
  • Look for signs of Cushing syndrome, pheochromocytoma, hyperaldosteronism, virilization, feminization.
  • Ask about previous history of cancer.

2. Biochemical Testing:

  • All patients:
    • 24-hour urinary fractionated catecholamines/metanephrines or plasma free metanephrines (screen for pheochromocytoma).
  • If hypertensive:
    • Measure plasma aldosterone and plasma renin activity (PRA) (screen for hyperaldosteronism).
  • Overnight 1-mg dexamethasone suppression test:
    • Screen for subclinical Cushing syndrome.

3. Imaging Characteristics:

  • CT scan:
    • Benign features: Size <3 cm, homogeneity, low density (Hounsfield units <10).
    • Malignant features: Size >5 cm, irregular borders, delayed contrast washout, heterogeneity.
  • MRI: Bright on T2-weighted images suggests pheochromocytoma.
Management
Indications for Resection
  • All functioning tumors should be excised.
  • Nonfunctioning tumors:
  • >5 cm: Resection due to higher malignancy risk.
  • <3 cm, homogeneous, low-density: Observe with serial imaging.
  • 3–5 cm: Decision based on patient age, comorbidities, and imaging features.
Special Considerations
  • History of Cancer:
  • Adrenal mass >3 cm: >50% chance of being metastatic.
  • Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) may help diagnose metastases if management will change, but:
    • Must rule out pheochromocytoma first (biochemical screening).
    • FNA is risky for adrenocortical carcinoma (risk of spreading cancer cells).
  • Solitary adrenal metastases:
  • Adrenalectomy can improve survival in:
    • Metastatic lung cancer (~25% 5-year survival if no other metastases).
    • Metastatic melanoma or renal cell carcinoma (even with other metastases).
  • Laparoscopic adrenalectomy is safe with minimal recurrence risk.
